name: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design
objective: Measure soot-inception limits, temperatures, soot volume fraction, and radiative or kinetic extinction limits of normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames, and test whether steady spherical diffusion flames can exist.
fuels: Gaseous ethylene (C2H4) and methane (CH4), diluted with nitrogen (N2) or carbon dioxide (CO2).
conditions: Drop-tower and ISS microgravity tests over varied pressures, flow rates, and reactant dilutions in both normal and inverse convection configurations.
variables: Varied fuel (C2H4 vs CH4), flow rate, stoichiometric mixture fraction (Zst), inert diluent amount (N2 or CO2), pressure, and convection direction (normal vs inverse).
sensors: Cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples.

findings.text: Flame Design measured soot across test conditions and showed that microgravity diffusion flames can be tuned to produce more or less soot.

Flame Design publications reported observations of long-duration microgravity spherical diffusion flames aboard the ISS and analyzed critical temperatures and mass fluxes for radiative extinction of ethylene flames at 1 bar.
Associated Flame Design studies reported water-gas shift equilibrium, double blue zones in normal and inverse jet flames, and elevated-pressure effects on hot, warm, and cool ethylene flames.

name: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator
objective: Establish quiescent microgravity burning and extinction limits on a porous gas burner calibrated to material properties, creating flammability maps linked to Cone Calorimeter (NASA Test 2) screening.
fuels: Gaseous methane/nitrogen (CH4/N2) and ethylene/nitrogen (C2H4/N2) mixtures on 25 mm and 50 mm porous circular burners emulating condensed-phase solids.
conditions: Quiescent microgravity aboard the ISS in O2/N2 and desired O2/CO2 ambients—including NASA mission atmospheres at 14.7 psia / 21% O2, 10.2 psia / 26.5% O2, and 8.2 psia / 34% O2—plus 1 g and drop-tower tests.
variables: Varied burner diameter (25 vs 50 mm), fuel/diluent mixture, ambient diluent (N2 vs CO2), oxygen concentration, pressure, and stepped-down fuel flow rate to find extinction.
sensors: Burner surface heat-flux and temperature-limit sensors plus optical flame observation.

findings.text: BRE observed quasi-steady burning emulating condensed-phase materials such as PMMA and Nylon in quiescent microgravity without airflow, challenging the practice of shutting off ventilation.
Sustained burning without airflow occurred mainly in elevated-oxygen spacecraft atmospheres, whereas flames in normal 21% oxygen self-extinguished quickly.
Preliminary results suggest NASA could expand use of Cone Calorimeter (Test 2) material property testing to relate ground screening to microgravity flammability maps.
NASA reported that the BRE investigation analyzed 59 burn tests aboard the ISS.

name: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II
objective: Investigate ignition, flame growth, spread, and extinction limits of realistic solid fuels in low-speed microgravity flow, bridge NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 to 0 g, and inform SoFIE requirements.
fuels: Solid fuels in practical geometries including slabs, rods, cylinders, spherical sections, films, and fabric sheets.
conditions: ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox wind tunnel at forced airflow speeds up to 40 cm/s in opposed and concurrent directions, with oxygen reduced below 21% via nitrogen dilution.
variables: Varied forced airflow speed and direction (opposed vs concurrent), ambient oxygen concentration, and sample material/geometry.
sensors: MSG optical imaging capturing flame appearance, flame growth, and spread rates.

findings.text: BASS-II was the first ISS investigation to dilute the glovebox with nitrogen for reduced-oxygen testing, and NASA sources note materials can burn at lower oxygen in microgravity than in normal gravity.

Across BASS-II tests reported in NASA/TM-20210011385, heat release averaged about 13.1 kJ per gram of O2 consumed, most burns stayed below 100 W, and the mean global equivalence ratio was fuel-rich near 1.3.
In microgravity, solid fuels burned as oval flames rather than buoyant upward cones, providing simpler geometry to evaluate combustion and fire-safety models.

Published BASS-II studies examined PMMA rod flammability boundaries in axial stagnation flow, critical flow velocities for opposed-flow radiative extinction, and concurrent composite-fabric quenching.

sensors: Top and edge visual flame observation recording flame size, shape, color, spread rate, and quenching.

findings.text: BASS results showed that NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 is not always conservative because materials can burn at lower oxygen concentrations in microgravity than on Earth.
Early BASS suppression tests demonstrated that directing a nitrogen jet onto a microgravity flame can strengthen burning by entraining surrounding oxygen.
In BASS tests at 17% oxygen compared to air, flames stayed blue longer with delayed soot formation.
Published BASS studies compared opposed-flow thermal regimes between 0 g and 1 g and analyzed boundary-layer blow-off extinction and fuel-thickness preheating effects.

name: Flame Extinguishment Experiment
objective: Map microgravity droplet Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) flammability boundaries, measure gaseous fire suppressant effectiveness (CO2, He, SF6), and validate reduced-gravity droplet extinction models.
fuels: Liquid fuel droplets (~3 mm and varied initial sizes), freely deployed or fiber-supported (fuel species not named in overview text).
conditions: ISS CIR/MDCA chamber primarily at 0.5–1.5 atm pressure, stepping ambient O2 mole fraction downward with CO2, He, or SF6 suppressants, mostly quiescent with slow droplet drift/translation tests.
variables: Varied pressure (0.5–1.5 atm), ambient oxygen mole fraction, suppressant gas (CO2, He, SF6), droplet diameter, deployment mode (free vs fiber), and sub-buoyant translation flow.
sensors: Optical diagnostics for droplet extinction diameter, burning rate, soot, flame radiation, and temperature profiles.

findings.text: FLEX showed that droplet limiting oxygen index (LOI) flammability limits are lower in reduced gravity, so terrestrial inert-gas suppressant standards do not offer the same safety margin in space.
FLEX discovered persistent low-temperature cool flames in which large alkane droplets continue vaporizing after the visible hot flame extinguishes.
NASA reported that FLEX cool flames persist longer in microgravity and produce carbon monoxide and formaldehyde rather than carbon dioxide and water.
FLEX publications reported two-stage cool-flame combustion in isolated microgravity n-heptane droplets and methanol droplet extinction in O2/CO2/N2 mixtures.

objective: Quantify liquid smoke droplet sizes from overheated spacecraft materials in microgravity, relate sizes to pyrolysis and transport, and build predictive smoke-growth code for spacecraft fire detectors.

findings.text: SAME showed that smoke particulate sizes in microgravity differ substantially from normal gravity, meaning terrestrial detectors look for different particle sizes than expected.
Secondary search snippets cited in research/01 report that a substantial share of SAME microgravity smoke particles were below about 500 nm and detection lags were longer in microgravity.
Published SAME studies reported low-gravity pyrolysis smoke particle-size measurements and evaluated spacecraft smoke-detector performance and ISS nuisance particulates.

findings.text: PSI-142 found that warm diffusion flames exhibit a double reaction zone structure that plays a critical role in transitions between cool flames and hot flames.

Published PSI-142 studies examined multistage warm diffusion flames and radical-index / oxygen-concentration effects on cool-flame extinction.
